paper_title: F2G-Pose: Geometry-Aware Foundation Feature Lifting for Direct RGB-D Category-Level Object Pose Estimation

sections.title: Abstract
sections.content: This paper studies category-level RGB-D object pose estimation, which recovers an object's 3D rotation and translation without instance-specific CAD models or reference views. This task is highly ambiguous due to intra-class variations, symmetries, and partial observations. Current solutions struggle to balance reliability and efficiency: methods based on intermediate structures are prone to error propagation, while diffusion models suffer from high inference latency and complex post-hoc candidate extraction. To address this, we present F2G-Pose, a real-time direct, single-pass framework that predicts category-level pose, metric size, and camera-frame completed shape from a single RGB-D observation in one feed-forward pass. F2G-Pose lifts dense visual foundation features to partial point clouds, encodes local geometry with DGCNN tokenization, and integrates object-level structure with a Mixture-of-Experts Transformer. Joint size prediction and camera-frame shape completion encourage metric consistency through dense geometric supervision. With its task-specific network trained only on pose-annotated synthetic SOPE data and its frozen RADIO backbone externally pretrained, F2G-Pose achieves state-of-the-art accuracy on SOPE and ROPE while running at 28 FPS for pose-only inference, and further demonstrates strong camera-frame geometry on HouseCat6D and real-object transfer on HANDAL. Analyses of latency, robustness, shape completion, and GenPose++ candidate behavior further demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of F2G-Pose, with real-world manipulation experiments demonstrating deployment potential under segmented RGB-D inputs. The project page, code, and pretrained models are made available at https://jrryzh.github.io/F2G-Pose/.

sections.title: 1 Introduction
sections.content: Category-level 6D object pose estimation recovers an objects 3D rotation and translation without requiring an instance-specific CAD model or reference views at test time. In practical RGB-D perception, this estimate is often coupled with metric size and usable object geometry for benchmark evaluation [9, 42, 51], physical interaction [6, 37, 38], and robotic control [14, 15, 24, 25, 44, 45]. This setting is inherently challenging because partial observations from single crop or segmented point cloud provide incomplete evidence: symmetries induce rotational ambiguity, occlusions hide discriminative geometry, and intra-class variations alter shape, size, and appearance. Consequently, category-level perception must produce reliable metric predictions from ambiguous, incomplete, and noisy observations. Equal contribution. Contact: zhangjinyu25@sii.edu.cn. Corresponding author. Contact: yanweifu@fudan.edu.cn. Preprint. Previous work has addressed this problem from two complementary directions. Deterministic category-level methods estimate pose and size through canonical coordinates [42], correspondences [2], shape priors [16], deformation models [39], alignment procedures [23], or direct regression [17, 26, 43]. While these methods enable efficient inference, reliance on intermediate structures can lead to compounding errors. Under occlusion, missing depth, intra-class variation, and domain shift, the final metric estimate can become sensitive to the reliability of these intermediate structures. Direct regression can avoid some post-hoc alignment steps, but reliable direct prediction still requires representations that preserve local geometric cues and global object structure under partial observations. complementary line of work models pose ambiguity explicitly. GenPose [50] and GenPose++ [51] formulate category-level pose estimation as conditional pose distribution modeling, sampling multiple hypotheses and converting them into prediction through scoring, filtering, clustering, or aggregation. This is principled for uncertainty representation, but it introduces candidate-to-decision gap: deployed accuracy depends not only on the sampled hypotheses, but also on whether post-hoc extraction can select or aggregate reliable representative. Moreover, this conversion must operate under practical inference budget as in Fig. 3, so sampling quality, candidate extraction, and computational cost become coupled. Joint-RegDiff [20] and RFMPose [32] improve generative pose inference through joint regressiondiffusion learning with score-scaling sampling and Riemannian flow-matching trajectories, respectively, but both still rely on iterative generative inference to produce the prediction, so prediction quality remains coupled with sampling dynamics, candidate extraction, and inference cost. We introduce F2G-Pose, direct RGB-D framework that jointly estimates category-level pose, size, and camera-frame completed geometry in single feed-forward pass. By leveraging geometry-aware foundation feature lifting and dense geometric supervision, it bypasses intermediate canonical shape alignment and avoids the sampling and candidate extraction used by sampling-based pose estimators. Specifically, we lift dense visual foundation features [13] to the partial point cloud for semantic cues, encode local geometry via DGCNN tokenization, and integrate object-level structure using Mixtureof-Experts Transformer that provides conditional capacity across diverse shape regimes. Then, the pose-size head predicts the final metric estimate, while the shape head reconstructs camera-frame geometry as both auxiliary supervision and usable output. This joint design encourages the shared representation to encode visible local evidence, object extent, and visible-to-complete geometric structure for consistent direct prediction under partial observations. To evaluate the effectiveness of this design, we train the task-specific network only on pose-annotated synthetic data from 149 SOPE categories [51] and test on SOPE [51], ROPE [51], HANDAL [10], and HouseCat6D [17]. These benchmarks cover synthetic benchmark accuracy, synthetic-to-real transfer, additional real-object evaluation, and camera-frame shape reconstruction. F2G-Pose achieves state-of-the-art accuracy while running at 28 FPS for pose inference. Beyond benchmark accuracy, we evaluate latency, robustness to perturbations and occlusion, shape reconstruction, GenPose++ candidate behavior, and real-world robotic manipulation. These results demonstrate the efficiency and reliability of direct feed-forward prediction, while robotic experiments demonstrate deployment potential under segmented RGB-D inputs. Contributions. Our contributions are threefold: (1) We present F2G-Pose, real-time direct RGB-D framework that predicts category-level 6D pose, metric size, and camera-frame completed shape in single feed-forward pass, sharing its representation across pose, size, and shape learning. (2) We introduce geometry-aware foundation feature lifting to map dense visual features onto partial point clouds. DGCNN encodes local geometry, Mixture-of-Experts Transformer integrates object-level structure, and camera-frame shape completion provides dense geometric supervision for metric prediction. (3) Extensive evaluations across synthetic benchmarks and real-world datasets demonstrate that F2G-Pose achieves state-of-the-art accuracy, real-time inference, and high-quality shape completion. Furthermore, physical manipulation experiments demonstrate pick-and-place success, timely decision readiness, and deployment feasibility under segmented RGB-D inputs.

sections.title: 2 Related work
sections.content: Category-Level 6D Pose Estimation. Category-level methods aim to generalize pose estimation across unseen object instances within category [17, 42, 43]. Early works such as NOCS [42] introduced the notion of canonical space to enable pose alignment without requiring CAD models. 2 Follow-up approaches [2, 23, 26, 50] leveraged point cloud geometry and symmetry-aware losses to improve generalization. Some methods further incorporate shape-aware modeling [16, 39] to jointly predict object size and shape. While these methods remove the need for object-specific models, many rely on intermediate canonical coordinates, correspondences, deformation fields, or shape priors whose reliability can degrade under occlusion, missing depth, and strong intra-category variation. Recent works have attempted to scale category-level 6D learning using larger and more diverse datasets [18, 53], making representation quality and inference efficiency increasingly important. Diffusion-based methods such as GenPose [50] and GenPose++ [51] model pose and size as multimodal distributions, but often rely on auxiliary scoring networks to filter outlier samples. JointRegDiff [20] eliminates the need for such scoring networks through time-dependent score scaling, and RFMPose [32] formulates generative category-level pose estimation with Riemannian flow matching; however, both remain limited to 6D pose estimation and still require iterative generative inference, which generally increases inference cost and can limit real-time throughput. SecondPose [3] also combines foundation-model features with geometry for direct category-level pose and size estimation through an SE(3)-consistent representation. F2G-Pose additionally predicts complete camera-frame shape to provide dense supervision for the shared pose-size representation, and uses MoE encoding to provide conditional capacity across diverse categories. Instance-Level Novel Object Pose Estimation. Another line of work estimates pose for novel object instances using CAD models [19, 30], single-view references, or multi-view references [11, 21, 27]. They often reconstruct object geometry, either explicitly via 3D modeling [22, 28] or implicitly through image-based retrieval [12, 29]. FoundationPose [46] supports either CAD or reference images, combining model-based and model-free paradigms. Recent foundation reconstruction models such as SAM 3D [35] reconstruct object geometry, texture, and layout from masked single images, targeting image-to-3D asset reconstruction in natural scenes. Together, these methods broaden objectcentric 3D perception, but generally target instance-specific reconstruction or reference-conditioned alignment rather than category-level pose-size estimation under fixed taxonomy. F2G-Pose targets this complementary category-level setting: it uses category-level canonical supervision during training, but requires only segmented RGB-D observation at inference time for the evaluated taxonomy.

sections.title: 3 Method
sections.content: Problem Formulation and Overview Given an RGB image crop RHW 3 and segmented partial point cloud RN 3, F2G-Pose predicts the objects 6D pose = (R, t) SE(3), metric size R3, and completed camera-frame shape Pdense RNd3 in single feed-forward pass, without requiring instance-specific CAD models, reference images, or explicit category labels. Here, SO(3) and R3 denote the object rotation and translation, respectively. The framework directly predicts the outputs, avoiding the test-time sampling and candidate extraction of sampling-based estimators, as shown in Fig. 1. Instead, it lifts dense visual foundation features onto observed 3D points, encodes local geometric structure with DGCNN, aggregates object-level context with MoE Transformer, and uses parallel decoder branches for pose-size prediction and camera-frame shape completion. The pose-size branch directly outputs the metric object state used for evaluation and downstream applications, while the shape branch provides dense geometric supervision for the shared RGB-D representation and produces approximate completed geometry in the camera frame.

sections.title: 3.1 Geometry-Aware Foundation Feature Lifting
sections.content: F2G-Pose uses RADIOv2.5 [13] to provide dense visual evidence for the partial RGB-D observation. RADIOv2.5 distills complementary 2D vision models [7, 31, 33, 34], combining dense feature extraction from SAM [34] with semantic features from DINOv2 [31]. Prior work has shown that DINOv2-style local features can support pose-consistent correspondences across object appearance and shape variation [52, 54]. We use these features not as standalone image prior, but as point-wise appearance and semantic cues attached to metric 3D observations. Given an RGB crop I, we fuse RADIOv2.5 layers {8, 16, 23} as Frgb = R(cid:0) (cid:80) αlCl(ERADIO(I)l)(cid:1) Rhw1024. Each 1 1 convolutional block Cl compresses its map to 512 channels; learned softmax-normalized weights αl combine the maps, and 3 3 convolutional block refines the sum to 1024 channels. 3 Figure 1: F2G-Pose Overview. Given cropped RGB image and segmented partial point cloud, F2G-Pose extracts dense RADIOv2.5 features [13] and lifts them onto 3D points by projection. DGCNN tokenization produces fused RGB-D object tokens, and MoE Transformer encodes global object representation. Two parallel decoder branches directly predict (i) 6D pose and metric size and (ii) camera-frame completed shape through coarse-to-fine refinement. The pipeline produces pose-size-shape estimate in one feed-forward pass. We then lift the dense image features onto the partial point cloud. For each point Pi, we gather fi = Frgb[π(Pi)/16] at its patch-grid index, where π() gives crop-pixel coordinates and 16 is the patch size. Following the point-wise fusion spirit of DenseFusion [41], we concatenate each 3D point with its lifted visual feature (denoted by ) and process the fused point set with Dynamic Graph Convolutional Neural Network (DGCNN) encoder EGCN(). This yields the fused embedding i=1) Rnd, which serves as local geometry-aware input tokens for the Ffuse = EGCN({Pi fi}N Transformer encoder, where = 128 and = 512 denote the number of tokens and the embedding dimension, respectively.

sections.title: 3.2 MoE-Based Object Encoding
sections.content: The DGCNN tokens encode local surface neighborhoods and point-wise visual cues. We process these tokens with stack of Transformer blocks with multi-head self-attention [40], following the use of Transformers for point cloud completion and geometry modeling [48, 49]. This stage integrates local evidence across the object crop to form an object-level representation for metric prediction. To increase representation capacity with conditional expert aggregation, we replace the standard feed-forward layers in each Transformer block with Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layers [4, 5, 8]. Each MoE layer contains an independent set of experts and uses linear gating network to compute softmax probabilities over Ne = 8 experts. For each token, we select the top-2 experts according to the gating scores, route the token to these experts, and aggregate their outputs using the selected probabilities renormalized to sum to one. soft load-balancing penalty encourages balanced gate probabilities during training [36]. Finally, the encoded tokens are aggregated by global pooling to produce compact object representation for direct 6D pose, size, and shape prediction.

sections.title: 3.3 Direct Pose-Size and Shape Decoding
sections.content: F2G-Pose uses two lightweight decoding branches on top of the shared object representation. The pose-size branch predicts the metric state directly, while the shape branch predicts complete geometry in the camera frame. Both branches are trained jointly, so dense geometric supervision can regularize the representation used for direct pose and size prediction without adding any test-time optimization or candidate extraction. Pose and Size Estimation. The pose-size branch regresses rotation, translation, and metric size directly from the global object representation. For rotation, we adopt the continuous 6D representation [56], which uses the first two columns of the rotation matrix SO(3) and reconstructs valid matrix via orthogonalization. This parameterization improves optimization stability while keeping the prediction deterministic and feed-forward. The branch outputs the final pose-size estimate directly, without sampling pose candidates or applying post-hoc aggregation. 4 Camera-Frame Shape Completion. From the extracted global feature vector, we first regress coarse complete object shape Pcoarse R5123 using lightweight MLP. Since the input partial point cloud contains observed metric geometry, we concatenate Pcoarse with farthest-point-sampled observations from to form combined point set, which is then processed through another MLP with Sigmoid activation to produce confidence score for each point. This selects reliable points for fusion, producing the refined fused point cloud Pfuse R5123. Finally, each point in Pfuse is augmented with the global feature vector and passed through an MLP to predict four local offsets per point, yielding Pdense R20483. The shape is reconstructed directly in the camera frame, providing geometry output and dense auxiliary signal for learning metric-consistent object representations.

sections.title: 3.4 Training Objectives
sections.content: Pose and Size Regression Loss. We supervise pose and size with Smooth L1 losses. For rotation, we account for object symmetries following the benchmark treatment in [51], so symmetry-equivalent rotations are treated as valid targets rather than arbitrary errors. Specifically, for each axis, an objects symmetry is categorized as no symmetry, 90-degree rotational symmetry, 180-degree rotational symmetry, or arbitrary-angle rotational symmetry. Based on this classification, we generate set of valid ground-truth rotation matrices and compare the predicted rotation against all candidates. The loss is computed with respect to the closest ground-truth rotation. sections.title: 4 Experiments
sections.content: Datasets. We use SOPE [51] as the training source for F2G-Pose; it contains 5K synthetic object instances from 149 categories with category-level canonical pose, metric size, and complete shape supervision. Pose-size evaluation uses SOPE and ROPE [51]: SOPE measures synthetic benchmark performance, while ROPE evaluates transfer to scanned real objects under the same category taxonomy. For camera-frame geometry evaluation, we use SOPE and HouseCat6D [17], where complete object geometry is available. For additional real-world transfer, we evaluate selected HANDAL objects [10], including hammers, mugs, pans, and wrench-like tools. The 92 instances from seven HANDAL categories map to six SOPE categories; selection follows taxonomy correspondence. Thus, ROPE and this HANDAL subset evaluate seen-category, unseen-instance transfer (Appendix B.4). Baselines and metrics. For category-level pose-size estimation, we compare with NOCS, SGPA, IST-Net, HS-Pose, GenPose, and GenPose++ using the SOPE/ROPE benchmark results reported by Omni6DPose [51]. Joint-RegDiff [20] and RFMPose [32] are report-only comparisons from their papers, using public metrics available under the SOPE/ROPE taxonomy. For reference-based comparisons on real datasets, we additionally report FoundationPose [46] and Any6D [21]. For runtime comparison, we benchmark executable methods under unified inference protocol using the same segmentation masks, RGB-D crops, depth preprocessing, batch size 1, and GPU-synchronized timing on one RTX 4090; accuracy results follow the evaluation sources specified above. Pose-size accuracy is evaluated with AUC of 3D bounding-box IoU at thresholds 25/50/75, VUS under joint rotation-translation thresholds, and mean rotation/translation error. Shape completion is evaluated using Chamfer-L1 distance.

sections.title: 4.1 Comparison with State-of-the-Art Methods
sections.content: Pose-size accuracy and latency. Table 1 shows that F2G-Pose improves the accuracy-latency operating point of category-level RGB-D pose estimation. On SOPE, F2G-Pose improves GenPose++ from 31.9 to 43.7 AUC at IoU50 and reduces mean rotation error from 19.9 to 15.7; on ROPE, it improves AUC across all IoU thresholds and matches or exceeds the available high-precision VUS results. This gain is not only speedup from removing iterative sampling. The larger improvement on IoU and rotation-sensitive metrics indicates that direct prediction benefits from stronger conditioning: dense image features preserve category and part cues, local point neighborhoods preserve observed surface evidence, and global token interactions integrate these cues into metric pose-size estimate. 6 Figure 2: Qualitative results on ROPE. We show the input RGB image, ground-truth pose, poses from GenPose++ and F2G-Pose, and the predicted camera-frame shape. Table 2: GenPose++ candidate diagnostics on ROPE. More qualitative examples are provided in Appendix A.7. Candidate-to-decision and time-budget analysis. Table 2 examines the candidate behavior of GenPose++ as strong generative baseline. Its candidate distribution is heavy-tailed: although the median rotation error is only 8, the mean rises to 39, with 26.9% of sampled candidates exceeding 45. With = 50 samples, an oracle selects candidate within 5 for 79.3% of instances, achieving median error of 1.78. However, deployed pipeline must still score, filter, cluster, or aggregate these candidates, so its final prediction can be substantially worse than the oracle. This highlights the candidate-to-decision gap discussed in the introduction: candidate-set quality and deployed prediction quality are related but not equivalent. Candidate quality also varies with object structure; no-symmetry objects have the largest mean rotation error, suggesting that sampling difficulty is driven not only by pose ambiguity but also by distinctive yet partially observed geometry. Additional candidate diagnostics by symmetry are provided in Appendix A.4. Figure 3 evaluates the same issue under real-time budget. Reducing diffusion candidates improves responsiveness but lowers final accuracy because candidate extraction becomes less reliable. F2GPose avoids this trade-off by optimizing the final pose-size decision directly. Geometry output and shape completion. Table 3 evaluates camera-frame geometry output. The point-completion baselines are trained on the SOPE training split with the same partial-to-complete camera-frame targets. Compared with these geometry-only baselines [4749], F2G-Pose achieves substantially lower Chamfer-L1 error on both SOPE and HouseCat6D. The qualitative results in Fig. 2 show that F2G-Pose successfully reconstructs complete object geometries. sections.title: 4.2 Ablation Studies
sections.content: Component ablation. Table 4 isolates the main design factors of F2G-Pose on ROPE. Removing RGB foundation features leads to the largest performance drop, particularly on the rotation-sensitive VUS metrics, showing that point-wise visual lifting provides pose-relevant appearance and semantic cues beyond partial geometry alone. Replacing the MoE Transformer with parameter-equivalent dense FFN also reduces accuracy, suggesting that conditional capacity helps model category-level object diversity. Removing auxiliary shape supervision further degrades pose-size prediction, indicating that dense camera-frame geometry supervision regularizes the shared RGB-D representation and directly benefits the final pose-size estimate. Representation analysis. Table 5 studies how different RGB-D representations affect direct posesize prediction. All variants are trained with the same pose-size losses, while varying the feature aggregation strategy, contextual encoder, foundation backbone, and the use of auxiliary shape 8 Table 7: Performance on reflective and transparent materials across ROPE and HouseCat6D.

Replacing global feature pooling with DGCNN tokens improves both IoU and rotationsensitive VUS, showing that local surface neighborhoods provide important geometric cues for direct pose estimation. Adding Transformer context further improves performance by integrating local RGBD evidence into an object-level representation. The full model achieves the best results, indicating that local geometric tokenization, object-level context, and camera-frame geometry supervision are complementary. Finally, replacing RADIO with DINOv2 or CLIP causes only modest degradation in IoU50, suggesting that the improvement is driven primarily by the architecture and supervision rather than by specific foundation backbone. Additional backbone, routing, and shape-decoder ablations are summarized in Appendix A.6. MoE routing analysis. Table 6 shows that top-2 MoE provides favorable accuracy-latency trade-off. Top-1 routing is faster but less accurate, while top-4 brings only marginal accuracy gains at higher latency cost. Compared with top-2 routing without balancing, the load-balanced top-2 MoE achieves higher routing entropy, lower load concentration, and better pose accuracy. These results suggest that balanced conditional capacity improves the shared RGB-D representation while keeping inference cost moderate. Further instance-level analysis finds overlapping category-related expert preferences (Appendix B.3). Robustness under challenging materials. Table 7 reports performance on transparent and reflective objects, which often corrupt depth observations. Compared with the overall ROPE performance, F2G-Pose shows moderate degradation on these material subsets, with reflective objects being more difficult than transparent ones, especially in VUS and Chamfer distance. The performance drop is most apparent in IoU75, where depth holes, specular artifacts, and missing thin structures can perturb the estimated object extent. similar trend is observed on HouseCat6D, where reconstruction remains accurate for many transparent objects because their shapes are regular despite noisy depth. Overall, F2G-Pose remains reasonably robust under material-induced sensing noise, while precise box alignment is still sensitive to imperfect depth observations. Controlled RGB and depth perturbation results are reported in Appendix A.3, with additional material examples in Fig. 9. SAM-mask and controlled erosion/dilation results are provided in Appendix B.2.

sections.title: 4.3 Real-World Evaluation and Deployment

On HANDAL, F2G-Pose outperforms the reference-free methods Any6D and GenPose++, while on ROPE it further surpasses the singlereference method FoundationPose and the referencefree method Any6D, without requiring an instance reference. These results complement the controlled SOPE/ROPE benchmark by exposing the model to additional real objects, masks, backgrounds, and sensor noise patterns. Robot manipulation. We validate the final pose-size decision in real pick-and-place setup using an ARX robotic arm, parallel-jaw gripper, and an external RealSense RGB-D camera. All methods receive the same object masks and RGB-D crops, and the evaluated objects include bottles, bowls, cans, mugs, cups, hammers, pans, and wrench-like tools. The predicted pose and metric size determine the grasp approach and placement target; the completed camera-frame shape is used only for collision checking. Each trial randomizes object placement within tabletop start region, and success requires grasping, transporting, and placing the object at the target without dropping or collision. The full model achieves 74/80 successful picks and 68/80 successful placements. Figure 4 illustrates the physical setup and representative trials, while Table 9 shows that F2G-Pose preserves high manipulation success while meeting real-time perception budget. GenPose++ is effective when run with its full sampling and clustering pipeline, but the full pipeline is too slow for the 50 ms control budget; reducing candidates improves responsiveness at the cost of lower pick-and-place success. The depth-only and w/o-shape variants further show that dense visual lifting and camera-frame shape supervision improve deployed pick-and-place success. Failure analysis. In qualitative benchmark cases, failures mainly occur when corrupted depth removes thin or asymmetric parts, severe occlusion hides functional geometry, or symmetric lowtexture objects admit 90/180 alternatives. Additional examples are shown in Appendix A.5.

sections.title: 5 Conclusion
sections.content: We present F2G-Pose, direct RGB-D framework that estimates category-level 6D pose, metric size, and camera-frame shape from single observation. By lifting dense visual foundation features to partial point clouds and encoding local-global geometry with MoE Transformer, F2G-Pose predicts the deployed pose-size state in one feed-forward pass. Experiments on SOPE, ROPE, HouseCat6D, HANDAL, and ARX manipulation show favorable balance of accuracy, inference latency, and manipulation success, while the shape branch provides dense geometric supervision and approximate planning geometry. Limitations. F2G-Pose assumes segmented RGB-D crop at inference time, so mask failures and severe depth corruption can propagate to pose, size, and shape. The method remains sensitive to thin or asymmetric parts, severe occlusion, and symmetric low-texture objects that admit multiple plausible rotations. High-precision metric alignment remains weak under cross-dataset domain shift, which may require downstream refinement for tasks with tight geometric tolerances. Symmetry-aware supervision does not eliminate ambiguity under severe occlusion or near-symmetry, and the model provides no calibrated uncertainty or abstention mechanism. Future work will address mask-free operation, broader real-object coverage, articulated or deformable categories, and active perception for heavy occlusion. Broader Impact. F2G-Pose advances category-level object perception for robotics and augmented reality. While improved pose estimation can benefit assistive manipulation and humanrobot collaboration, it could also be applied in surveillance or autonomous systems without adequate safety oversight. We encourage responsible deployment with appropriate human supervision.

sections.title: A Additional Implementation Details
sections.content: A.1 Model Details F2G-Pose receives segmented RGB crop and its corresponding partial point cloud. We sample 1024 points from the segmented depth observation and concatenate each point coordinate with lifted visual feature. Frozen RADIOv2.5-L [13] provides feature maps from layers 8, 16, and 23. Independent 1 1 convolutional blocks compress each map from 1024 to 512 channels. Learned softmax-normalized layer weights combine them by summation, followed by 3 3 convolutional block producing 1024 channels; both convolutional stages use BatchNorm and ReLU. We gather each points feature by integer-dividing its crop-pixel coordinates by the patch size of 16. This produces an input tensor of size 1024 1027. The fused RGB-D point set is tokenized by DGCNN encoder with two downsampling stages, reducing 1024 input points to 128 object tokens. The tokens are projected to 512 dimensions and processed by 8 Transformer blocks with 8 attention heads. In the full model, each Transformer feed-forward layer is replaced by top-2 Mixture-of-Experts layer with 8 experts and the loadbalancing loss described in the main paper. learned softmax-weighted sum combines the block outputs; an MLP projects the tokens to 1024 dimensions before max pooling. The pose-size branch directly regresses rotation, translation, and metric size. The shape branch predicts 512 initial points, concatenates 256 farthest-point-sampled observed points, scores the 768 candidates and retains 512, then predicts four local offsets per retained point for 2048-point completed shape. The selected 512 points and final 2048 points receive reconstruction supervision. Continuous rotational symmetries use 1 candidate sampling; objects with at least two continuously symmetric axes are excluded from the rotation loss. A.2 Training Details F2G-Pose is trained only on the SOPE training split used in the main experiments. We train for 100 epochs with batch size 512 using AdamW. The initial learning rate is 104, the weight decay is 5 104, and LambdaLR schedule decays the learning rate by factor of 0.9 every 8 epochs with lower bound of 2% of the initial value. BatchNorm momentum is decayed from 0.9 by factor of 0.5 every 3 epochs with minimum value of 0.01. Training experiments are run with PyTorch 2.4 and CUDA 12.4 using automatic mixed precision, DistributedDataParallel, and synchronized BatchNorm on 4 NVIDIA H200 GPUs. For runtime comparison, we benchmark executable methods under unified inference protocol using the same segmentation masks, RGB-D crops, depth preprocessing, batch size 1, and GPUsynchronized timing on one RTX 4090. The pose-only setting disables the shape head after the shared RGB-D encoder, while the full setting keeps the shape branch enabled. A.3 Controlled Robustness Evaluation To complement the material robustness study in the main paper, we evaluate controlled perturbations on ROPE. RGB perturbations simulate common photometric changes, while depth perturbations simulate sensor noise. These results are intended as stress tests of the current SOPE-trained model rather than as separate dataset contribution. Photometric perturbations. For RGB inputs, we apply exposure shifts (0.5/ 1.3/ 2.2 EV), white-balance shifts (800/ 2000/ 4000 K), and synthetic illumination changes (gradient or vignetting at 0.10/0.25/0.40 strength). Table 10 shows that performance changes only mildly under light and moderate perturbations, while heavy perturbations produce larger but still bounded drop. Depth perturbations. For depth inputs, we inject heteroscedastic noise σ(z) = α + βz2, where α {0.001, 0.002, 0.003} and β {0.000, 0.003, 0.006}. As summarized in Table 11, depth noise affects the method more strongly than photometric shifts, consistent with the main papers observation that precise metric alignment is sensitive to corrupted or missing depth. 15 Figure 5: Examples of controlled RGB and depth perturbations. The oracle best-of-50 result in the main paper indicates that the candidate set often contains accurate hypotheses, but the breakdown shows that candidate quality is uneven across object structures. Objects without rotational symmetry are especially difficult: they have fewer near-perfect candidates and larger average rotation error, so post-hoc scoring or clustering has harder selection problem. Table 12: GenPose++ candidate quality by symmetry on ROPE. Values are computed over sampled candidates before the final candidate extraction step. Symmetry type Mean rotation error Candidates 5 Continuous Quarter-turn Half-turn None 49% 33% 25% 21% 24.0 19.0 45.0 57.0 A.5 Failure Mode Analysis The qualitative failure cases are drawn from ROPE and are consistent with the limitations stated in the paper: corrupted depth on thin or reflective structures, heavy occlusion, and ambiguous rotations for symmetric or weakly textured objects. Reflective and transparent materials. Reflective or transparent surfaces often produce missing or distorted depth. RADIO features provide complementary appearance cues, but they cannot fully recover metric extent when the observed point cloud loses thin handles, sharp edges, or asymmetric parts. This leads to high-precision IoU and rotation errors, as shown in Fig. 6. Occlusion. Under mild or moderate occlusion, the model can often infer pose from visible geometry and lifted semantic cues. Severe occlusion removes too much task-relevant evidence, especially when the hidden region contains the asymmetric part needed to disambiguate orientation. Category ambiguity. For symmetric, regular, or small low-texture objects, multiple rotations can be visually plausible from single RGB-D observation. The model may therefore predict symmetry-related or near-symmetry-related orientation, producing typical 90 or 180 errors as illustrated in Fig. 7. Figure 6: Failure cases caused by corrupted or incomplete depth on reflective object regions. Figure 7: Failure cases caused by symmetric, geometrically regular, or small objects with ambiguous orientation cues. A.6 Supplementary Ablation Results Table 13 summarizes additional ablations while avoiding new claims beyond the current method. The RGB ablation confirms that lifted foundation features are major contributor under partial depth. The MoE variants show that top-2 routing is the adopted trade-off: top-4 gives only marginal gain over top-2 at higher cost, while top-1 is faster but less accurate. The backbone variants show that the framework remains effective with DINOv2 or CLIP, although RADIO gives the best result. The shape-decoder variants indicate that point selection and coarse-to-fine refinement also affect pose-size accuracy through the shared representation. 17 Table 13: Supplementary pose-size ablations on ROPE. sections.content: B.1 Matched RGB-D Shape Completion The camera-frame comparison in Table 3 measures the complete prediction system: its Chamfer distance includes intrinsic reconstruction error and global pose, translation, and scale error. Moreover, the geometry-only baselines and F2G-Pose receive different input information and supervision. B.3 MoE Expert Preferences Beyond load balance, we analyze instance-level routing over 7,466 object samples. Routing exhibits an association with category (Cramérs = 0.306, < 0.001). Different experts show preferences for broad geometry-related groups, including bag-like, flat, and bowl-like objects, with substantial overlap. This suggests distributed specialization rather than rigid one-expert-per-category partition. Associations with material and visibility are weaker, and no significant independent association with symmetry was found. These observations complement the capacity and balance analysis in Table 6. B.4 HANDAL Selection and Per-Category Results HANDAL is an independent real-world dataset with sensing conditions, capture environments, and object instances distinct from SOPE. The remaining categories have ambiguous mappings or no direct SOPE counterparts and are excluded because no corresponding canonical frame is defined. B.5 Reference-Free and Single-Reference Evaluation Protocols Any6D (zero reference). Zero reference means that no additional reference view is supplied beyond the test RGB-D observation. We use the official repositorys reference-free image-to-3D pathway, which reconstructs coarse shape from the test observation and subsequently estimates pose using that reconstructed shape. Any6D (one reference). We randomly sample one additional view of the same object from its ROPE multi-view sequence as the reference image and apply the standard reference-query inference protocol. FoundationPose (one reference). We evaluate the model-free pathway under the same onereference constraint. One additional real view of the same object is randomly sampled from its ROPE sequence; an object mesh is reconstructed from that view and used for pose estimation.
